scenes.visual: Scallop in rock and a beach scallop look alike; the question appears.
scenes.tts: Virginia's state fossil is a scallop shell. It is millions of years old. Yet it looks a lot like a scallop shell on a beach today. How do scientists know that living things have changed over time, and are related?

scenes.visual: Fossil examples, the fossil record with gaps, extinct, trilobites.
scenes.tts: A fossil is the preserved remains or traces of a living thing from the past. Shells, bones, teeth and footprints can all be fossils. Fossils are rare, so the fossil record, all the fossils found so far, has gaps. Even so, it shows many kinds of life that are not alive now. A group is extinct when no living members are left. Trilobites are extinct.

scenes.tts: Here is one well-known early fossil for each group. It is not the oldest one found. Early fish, about 518 million years old. Four-legged animals, about 365 million. Mammal relatives, about 205 million. Bird-like dinosaurs, about 150 million.

scenes.visual: Same set of bones in four limbs; common ancestor.
scenes.tts: Your arm has one upper arm bone, two lower arm bones, wrist bones and finger bones. A cat's front leg, a whale's flipper and a bat's wing have the same set. The shapes differ, and the jobs differ. A common ancestor is an early population. Two or more kinds of living things came from it. A shared ancestor with these bones explains the match best.

scenes.visual: DNA sequence rows; changes collect; recent versus earlier split.
scenes.tts: D N A gives a second check. A D N A sequence is the order of the bases A, T, C and G along a piece of D N A. Small changes in D N A happen and get passed on. Species that split from a common ancestor more recently have had less time to collect changes. So closer relatives usually have more similar D N A.

scenes.visual: Theory defined; three evidence chips converge on one story.
scenes.tts: In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation backed by many lines of evidence. It is not a guess. The theory of evolution says living things change over time and share common ancestors. It predicts that fossils, bones and D N A will tell the same family story. Each one could have told a different story. Instead, they largely agree. That is how scientists know.
